lessons.title: What Is Claude Code
lessons.summary: An agentic CLI that reads your repo, edits files, runs tests, and commits — all with permission gates you control.
body: Claude Code is not autocomplete. It is an agent that operates a real terminal: it reads files, runs commands, writes code, and waits for your approval at each risky step. It lives in your terminal first, but the same agent now runs in the VS Code and JetBrains extensions, a desktop app, and on the web at claude.ai/code — everything in this course transfers.

The mental shift: instead of typing characters, you describe outcomes. Instead of clicking Run, you watch the agent run things and read back the output. Instead of debugging line by line, you tell it what's broken and it iterates until tests pass.

Vibe coding is the practice of working at this altitude. You stay in flow on the *what*, the agent handles the *how*. The skills you'll build in this course are the prompts, patterns, and guardrails that make this loop reliable.

quiz.q: Which of these best describes Claude Code?
options: An IDE plugin that autocompletes code as you type.
A CLI agent that reads your repo, runs commands, and edits files with your permission.
A SaaS that hosts your code in the cloud and runs tests there.
A code review bot that comments on GitHub PRs.
quiz.explanation: Claude Code runs locally on your machine as a CLI. It can read files, run shell commands, and edit code, but every potentially-destructive action is gated by an approval prompt.

quiz.q: What is the core mental shift of "vibe coding"?
options: Letting the AI ship code with no oversight.
Typing prompts in natural language instead of code.
Operating at the level of outcomes; the agent handles the how.
Replacing your editor with a chat window.
quiz.explanation: You describe the outcome you want — a feature, a fix, a refactor — and let the agent do the file edits, test runs, and grep work. You still review every change.

lessons.title: Install the CLI
lessons.summary: Get Claude Code running on your machine and verify the install.

content.text: You need a Claude account with a **Pro or Max plan** (or an Anthropic API key). The install itself is free — the agent needs the account to think with.
Verify with `claude --version` — a version number means the CLI is on your PATH and ready.

content.title: Which install method should I pick?
content.text: The native installer (curl/PowerShell) is recommended — no Node.js required and it self-updates cleanly. Use the npm route only if you already live in a Node toolchain and prefer managing it there.

steps.title: Install the CLI
steps.body: Pick your platform in the tabs above and run the one-liner. The native installer is the recommended path — no Node.js required.
steps.copy: claude --version
steps.verify: A version number prints. If `command not found`, open a fresh terminal so PATH changes load.

steps.title: Authenticate
steps.body: Launch Claude Code from any directory. The first run opens a browser window for OAuth login with your Claude account.
steps.copy: claude
steps.verify: After login the prompt becomes interactive and shows your working directory in the header.

steps.title: Pick a project
steps.body: Quit (Ctrl+C twice) and re-run `claude` from inside an existing repo. The directory you launch from becomes the working tree the agent can read and edit.
steps.copy:
cd ~/code/your-project
claude
steps.verify: The header shows the project path. Type "hi" to confirm the agent responds.

steps.title: Try a smoke test
steps.body: Ask the agent to describe your repo. If it can list files and summarize the structure, your install is healthy.
steps.copy: What does this repo do? Read package.json and the README, then summarize in 3 lines.
steps.verify: You should see a Read tool call against your files, then a 3-line summary.

quiz.q: Which folder becomes Claude Code's working tree?
options: Your home directory, always.
Whichever directory you launched `claude` from.
A sandbox folder Claude creates automatically.
Any folder you give it the absolute path to.
quiz.explanation: Claude Code uses your launch directory as the project root. Files outside that root are not visible to it unless you give it explicit access.

lessons.title: Your First Conversation
lessons.summary: Watch the agentic loop in action: a single prompt, a tool call, a result, an answer. This is the heartbeat.
body: Every Claude Code interaction is a loop. You speak. The agent decides if it needs information from your machine. If yes, it calls a tool — Read, Bash, Grep — and waits for the result. Then it speaks again, and the loop continues until the task is done.
Below is a sandbox replay of a real first conversation. Watch how the agent uses Read to actually look at the file before answering — this is what separates an agent from autocomplete.

lessons.title: The Agentic Loop
lessons.summary: Plan → act → observe → adjust. Understanding this loop is the difference between fighting the agent and flowing with it.
body: Every step the agent takes follows the same four-beat rhythm. Plan: decide what to do next based on the current goal and context. Act: call a tool — read a file, run a command, edit code. Observe: read the tool's output. Adjust: update the plan based on what came back, then loop.

When you understand this rhythm, two things happen. First, you stop interrupting mid-loop — you let the agent finish its observation before adding new constraints. Second, you start writing prompts that *front-load* the constraints, because constraints added before a loop starts are cheap; constraints added in the middle force a re-plan.

Concretely: 'Refactor the auth module. Keep the public API stable. Add tests for every changed file.' is a complete loop input. 'Refactor the auth module' followed by 'oh and don't break the API' two minutes later is a re-plan that costs you turns.

transcript.text: Add a /health endpoint to the API. It should return {status: 'ok'} and have a test.
Plan: find the API entry point, add the route, add a test. Acting now.
src/server.ts
I see Express. Adding the /health route and a Jest test next to existing tests.
Edit applied successfully.
Wrote 18 lines.

PASS  src/server.test.ts
Tests: 1 passed.
Done. /health returns {status:'ok'} and the new test passes. Two files changed.

quiz.q: Which sequence describes one beat of the agentic loop?
options: Plan, act, observe, adjust.
Read, edit, commit, push.
Prompt, generate, validate, deploy.
Think, write, test, review.
quiz.explanation: Plan: decide. Act: call a tool. Observe: read result. Adjust: update the plan. Then loop.

quiz.q: Why is front-loading constraints in your prompt cheaper than adding them later?
options: It uses fewer tokens overall.
Constraints added mid-loop force a re-plan, throwing away work that was done under the wrong assumption.
Late constraints are ignored.
Front-loaded constraints unlock a faster model.
quiz.explanation: If the agent has already read three files and started editing under one set of rules, a new constraint can invalidate that work. Stating constraints up front avoids the re-plan cost.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md and Project Memory
lessons.summary: Project-level instructions the agent loads automatically. The single highest-leverage file in your repo when you work this way.
body: Every time you launch Claude Code in a directory that has a CLAUDE.md, the file is injected into the agent's context. It's how you teach the agent your conventions, your stack, and your taste — once, durably.

Good CLAUDE.md files are short and specific: things the agent could not figure out by reading the code. Bad CLAUDE.md files restate what's obvious from package.json. The /init slash command writes a starter file you then prune. Mid-session, start any message with `#` to fold a new rule into memory without breaking flow.

steps.title: Run /init in a real project
steps.body: From inside a project with code, type /init. The agent reads your repo and proposes a CLAUDE.md.
steps.copy: /init
steps.verify: A CLAUDE.md appears at your project root with sections like 'Stack' and 'Conventions'.

steps.title: Trim aggressively
steps.body: Open the generated file. Delete anything obvious from package.json (frameworks, scripts). Keep only: hidden conventions, deploy quirks, and rules you've corrected the agent on before.
steps.copy:
# Project notes

## Stack quirks
- We use pnpm workspaces; never run `npm install`.
- The mobile package depends on a private registry — set NPM_TOKEN before installing.

## House style
- Tests live next to source as `*.test.ts`, not in `__tests__`.
- Prefer named exports; default exports only for Next.js page files.
- No console.log in committed code; use the logger in lib/log.ts.
steps.verify: Your CLAUDE.md is under ~30 lines and every line says something the agent could not infer.

steps.title: Test that it took
steps.body: Quit and relaunch claude in the same directory. Ask a question whose answer requires the file.
steps.copy: What package manager does this repo use, and why?
steps.verify: The agent answers "pnpm — npm install would corrupt the workspaces" without reading any other file.

steps.title: Add a personal layer
steps.body: Create ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for cross-project preferences (your tone, your default test framework). It loads on every project, layered under the project file.
steps.copy:
# My preferences
- Keep responses terse; no end-of-turn summaries.
- Default to TypeScript when language is ambiguous.
- When suggesting libraries, prefer the smallest dependency that works.
steps.verify: These rules now apply in every Claude Code session you open.

quiz.q: What belongs in CLAUDE.md?
options: Everything in package.json restated in prose.
Things the agent cannot figure out from reading the code: hidden conventions, deploy quirks, taste rules you've already corrected once.
A full architecture overview, multiple pages.
Your API keys and secrets.
quiz.explanation: CLAUDE.md is for the non-obvious. Anything inferable from the codebase belongs in the codebase. Anything secret never goes in CLAUDE.md.

quiz.q: Where does the personal layer live?
options: In every CLAUDE.md, copy-pasted.
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — loaded on every project, under the project file.
.vscode/settings.json.
It doesn't exist; CLAUDE.md is project-only.
quiz.explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is your global layer. Project CLAUDE.md overrides it where they conflict.

body: Claude Code is not autocomplete. It is an agent that operates a real terminal: it reads files, runs commands, writes code, and waits for your approval at each risky step. A code review bot that comments on GitHub PRs.

Replacing your editor with a chat window.

body: Claude Code is not autocomplete. It is an agent that operates a real terminal: it reads files, runs commands, writes code, and waits for your approval at each risky step. lessons.summary: Plan → act → observe → adjust. Understanding this loop is the difference between fighting the agent and flowing with it.
body: Every step the agent takes follows the same four-beat rhythm. Plan: decide what to do next based on the current goal and context. Act: call a tool — read a file, run a command, edit code. Observe: read the tool's output. Adjust: update the plan based on what came back, then loop.

body: Claude Code is not autocomplete. It is an agent that operates a real terminal: it reads files, runs commands, writes code, and waits for your approval at each risky step. A code review bot that comments on GitHub PRs.

Typing prompts in natural language instead of code.
Operating at the level of outcomes; the agent handles the how.
Replacing your editor with a chat window.
quiz.explanation: You describe the outcome you want — a feature, a fix, a refactor — and let the agent do the file edits, test runs, and grep work. You still review every change.

lessons.title: Install the CLI
lessons.summary: Get Claude Code running on your machine and verify the install.

content.text: You need a Claude account with a **Pro or Max plan** (or an Anthropic API key). The install itself is free — the agent needs the account to think with.
Verify with `claude --version` — a version number means the CLI is on your PATH and ready.

content.title: Which install method should I pick?
content.text: The native installer (curl/PowerShell) is recommended — no Node.js required and it self-updates cleanly. Use the npm route only if you already live in a Node toolchain and prefer managing it there.

steps.title: Install the CLI
steps.body: Pick your platform in the tabs above and run the one-liner. The native installer is the recommended path — no Node.js required.
steps.copy: claude --version
steps.verify: A version number prints. If `command not found`, open a fresh terminal so PATH changes load.

steps.title: Authenticate
steps.body: Launch Claude Code from any directory. The first run opens a browser window for OAuth login with your Claude account.
steps.copy: claude
steps.verify: After login the prompt becomes interactive and shows your working directory in the header.

steps.title: Pick a project
steps.body: Quit (Ctrl+C twice) and re-run `claude` from inside an existing repo. The directory you launch from becomes the working tree the agent can read and edit.
steps.copy:
cd ~/code/your-project
claude
steps.verify: The header shows the project path. Type "hi" to confirm the agent responds.

steps.title: Try a smoke test
steps.body: Ask the agent to describe your repo. If it can list files and summarize the structure, your install is healthy.
steps.copy: What does this repo do? Read package.json and the README, then summarize in 3 lines.
steps.verify: You should see a Read tool call against your files, then a 3-line summary.

quiz.q: Which folder becomes Claude Code's working tree?
options: Your home directory, always.
Whichever directory you launched `claude` from.
A sandbox folder Claude creates automatically.
Any folder you give it the absolute path to.
quiz.explanation: Claude Code uses your launch directory as the project root. Files outside that root are not visible to it unless you give it explicit access.

lessons.title: Your First Conversation
lessons.summary: Watch the agentic loop in action: a single prompt, a tool call, a result, an answer. This is the heartbeat.
body: Every Claude Code interaction is a loop. You speak. The agent decides if it needs information from your machine. If yes, it calls a tool — Read, Bash, Grep — and waits for the result. Then it speaks again, and the loop continues until the task is done.
Below is a sandbox replay of a real first conversation. Watch how the agent uses Read to actually look at the file before answering — this is what separates an agent from autocomplete.

transcript.text: Open the README and tell me what this project does in one sentence.
I'll read the README first, then summarize.

# Vibe Code School

An interactive curriculum for learning agentic AI tools end-to-end. Tracks include Claude Code, Codex for mobile, Antigravity for agents, Claude Cowork, and ChatGPT Work.
It's an interactive curriculum that teaches three agentic coding tools — Claude Code, Codex for mobile, and Antigravity — end to end.
Are there any failing tests?
Let me check by running the test suite.

PASS  app/courses/page.test.tsx
PASS  components/site-header.test.tsx

Tests: 2 passed, 2 total
Time: 1.4s
Two tests, both passing. The suite is green.

quiz.q: Why did the agent use Read before summarizing?
options: It was required by the system prompt.
It needed the actual file contents to give a grounded answer instead of guessing.
Read is faster than its built-in knowledge.
It always reads README.md before doing anything else.
quiz.explanation: An agent grounds its answers in real evidence. If it can read the file, it should — guessing from a project name is exactly the failure mode tools were built to prevent.

quiz.q: What was the loop in this conversation?
options: User → Read → Done.
User → Assistant decision → Tool call → Tool result → Assistant answer.
Assistant → User → Tool → Done.
Tool → User → Assistant → Tool.
quiz.explanation: Every turn the agent decides whether it needs evidence. If yes, it calls a tool and waits. If no, it answers from context. That cycle repeats until the task is complete.

lessons.title: The Agentic Loop
lessons.summary: Plan → act → observe → adjust. Understanding this loop is the difference between fighting the agent and flowing with it.
body: Every step the agent takes follows the same four-beat rhythm. Plan: decide what to do next based on the current goal and context. Act: call a tool — read a file, run a command, edit code. Observe: read the tool's output. Adjust: update the plan based on what came back, then loop.

When you understand this rhythm, two things happen. First, you stop interrupting mid-loop — you let the agent finish its observation before adding new constraints. Second, you start writing prompts that *front-load* the constraints, because constraints added before a loop starts are cheap; constraints added in the middle force a re-plan.

Concretely: 'Refactor the auth module. Keep the public API stable. Add tests for every changed file.' is a complete loop input. 'Refactor the auth module' followed by 'oh and don't break the API' two minutes later is a re-plan that costs you turns.

transcript.text: Add a /health endpoint to the API. It should return {status: 'ok'} and have a test.
Plan: find the API entry point, add the route, add a test. Acting now.
src/server.ts
I see Express. Adding the /health route and a Jest test next to existing tests.
Edit applied successfully.
Wrote 18 lines.

PASS  src/server.test.ts
Tests: 1 passed.
Done. /health returns {status:'ok'} and the new test passes. Two files changed.

quiz.q: Which sequence describes one beat of the agentic loop?
options: Plan, act, observe, adjust.
Read, edit, commit, push.
Prompt, generate, validate, deploy.
Think, write, test, review.
quiz.explanation: Plan: decide. Act: call a tool. Observe: read result. Adjust: update the plan. Then loop.

quiz.q: Why is front-loading constraints in your prompt cheaper than adding them later?
options: It uses fewer tokens overall.
Constraints added mid-loop force a re-plan, throwing away work that was done under the wrong assumption.
Late constraints are ignored.
Front-loaded constraints unlock a faster model.
quiz.explanation: If the agent has already read three files and started editing under one set of rules, a new constraint can invalidate that work. Stating constraints up front avoids the re-plan cost.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md and Project Memory
lessons.summary: Project-level instructions the agent loads automatically. The single highest-leverage file in your repo when you work this way.
body: Every time you launch Claude Code in a directory that has a CLAUDE.md, the file is injected into the agent's context. It's how you teach the agent your conventions, your stack, and your taste — once, durably.

Good CLAUDE.md files are short and specific: things the agent could not figure out by reading the code. Bad CLAUDE.md files restate what's obvious from package.json. The /init slash command writes a starter file you then prune. Mid-session, start any message with `#` to fold a new rule into memory without breaking flow.

steps.title: Run /init in a real project
steps.body: From inside a project with code, type /init. The agent reads your repo and proposes a CLAUDE.md.
steps.copy: /init
steps.verify: A CLAUDE.md appears at your project root with sections like 'Stack' and 'Conventions'.

steps.title: Trim aggressively
steps.body: Open the generated file. Delete anything obvious from package.json (frameworks, scripts). Keep only: hidden conventions, deploy quirks, and rules you've corrected the agent on before.
steps.copy:
# Project notes

## Stack quirks
- We use pnpm workspaces; never run `npm install`.
- The mobile package depends on a private registry — set NPM_TOKEN before installing.

## House style
- Tests live next to source as `*.test.ts`, not in `__tests__`.
- Prefer named exports; default exports only for Next.js page files.
- No console.log in committed code; use the logger in lib/log.ts.
steps.verify: Your CLAUDE.md is under ~30 lines and every line says something the agent could not infer.

steps.title: Test that it took
steps.body: Quit and relaunch claude in the same directory. Ask a question whose answer requires the file.
steps.copy: What package manager does this repo use, and why?
steps.verify: The agent answers "pnpm — npm install would corrupt the workspaces" without reading any other file.

steps.title: Add a personal layer
steps.body: Create ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for cross-project preferences (your tone, your default test framework). It loads on every project, layered under the project file.
steps.copy:
# My preferences
- Keep responses terse; no end-of-turn summaries.
- Default to TypeScript when language is ambiguous.
- When suggesting libraries, prefer the smallest dependency that works.
steps.verify: These rules now apply in every Claude Code session you open.

quiz.q: What belongs in CLAUDE.md?
options: Everything in package.json restated in prose.
Things the agent cannot figure out from reading the code: hidden conventions, deploy quirks, taste rules you've already corrected once.
A full architecture overview, multiple pages.
Your API keys and secrets.
quiz.explanation: CLAUDE.md is for the non-obvious. Anything inferable from the codebase belongs in the codebase. Anything secret never goes in CLAUDE.md.

quiz.q: Where does the personal layer live?
options: In every CLAUDE.md, copy-pasted.
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — loaded on every project, under the project file.
.vscode/settings.json.
It doesn't exist; CLAUDE.md is project-only.
quiz.explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is your global layer. Project CLAUDE.md overrides it where they conflict.
